article.title: Cognitive Abilities, Personality, and Sustainable Attitudes and Behavior
article.abstract: Climate change demands urgent action, yet individual engagement in sustainable behaviors remains inconsistent. We conducted two studies (N1 = 280, N2 = 973) examining how political orientation, personality traits, reasoning ability, social-emotional-behavioral skills, and complex problem solving relate to sustainable attitudes and behaviors in U.S. adults. Using structural equation modeling, we found that openness to experience was the strongest predictor, alongside liberal political orientation and self-perceived social engagement and innovation skills. Unexpectedly, both cognitive personality traits showed negative associations with sustainability outcomes, challenging the notion that cognitive abilities universally facilitate adaptive behavior. For sustainable behavior, these associations were small to moderate (-.25 <= r <= -.15) and most pronounced for food-related and engagement-related behaviors. Specification curve analyses confirmed that less established constructs (social, emotional, and behavioral skill self-concepts and complex problem solving) contributed meaningful variance beyond established personality predictors and that these associations were robust across analytical specifications. Overall, psychological characteristics together explained up to 44\\% of variance in sustainable attitudes and 29\\% of variance in sustainable behavior. These findings advance our understanding of the psychological underpinnings of environmental engagement and highlight the need for future research to clarify the mechanisms underlying the negative cognitive ability-sustainability association.
article.authors: Lubczyk, Till and Bleidorn, Wiebke and Hopwood, Christopher J. and Kretzschmar, Andre

samples.occasion_label: Single assessment conducted over two sessions
samples.notes: Reference analytic N=973 in the author-selected Study 2 dataset (PDF pp.10-11; public original-item data verified against the source manifest). Private-comment exclusions cannot be independently reconstructed. 23 released records have the entire HEXACO block missing. Pearson correlations use available pairs; pair N ranges 790-973. Reference N remains 973; no participants are removed for missing age or the binary sex/gender contrast. Male=0 and female=1; other categories/nonresponse are missing only for that contrast. Age range 18-49 is coded adult under the mixed-adult convention. The two sessions measured different constructs rather than repeated SEB waves. BESSI-96 form type retains the historical long classification. Distinct persuasion/perspective scoring was confirmed by the user on 2026-11-04; domain weights are normalised to retain the 1-5 metric. Observed task components and questionnaire means are retained separately from latent factors. The pairwise matrix has a small negative minimum eigenvalue (-4.1337e-05); observed correlations were not repaired. Extraction audits are under extraction/0145; current analytical integration status is recorded separately in integration/batches.csv and integration/matrices.csv.
